newsitem.title: BOSNIA: A year on, Sarajevo's torched Grbavica zone bustles.
newsitem.headline: A year on, Sarajevo's torched Grbavica zone bustles.

text.p: A year ago, the Sarajevo district of Grbavica was a torched, derelict area ransacked by angry Serbs who fled the Bosnian capital rather than live under Moslem-Croat rule.
Despite the destruction, it was immediately taken over by thousands of jubilant Sarajevans anxious to claim the last of the five Serb-held suburbs acquired through the Bosnian peace agreement.
Having Grbavica released from Bosnian Serb control meant Sarajevo was a unified city after four years of division into warring ghettoes.

When Moslem-Croat police entered Grbavica on March 19 last year, they found fires still smouldering in apartments and a few residents peering from shelters which protected them against the rage of the departing Serbs.
Today, Grbavica and other parts of Sarajevo offer a different picture.
What was a dingy, half-burned line of shops in Grbavica is now a freshly painted market place with shops full of brisk trading and housewifes arguing with shopkeepers over vegetable prices.
"We found 2,100 people in Grbavica last year, now there are more than 18,000 living here," a district official told Reuters, noting that the pre-war population was 25,000.

In Grbavica, as in the four other returned areas, people threw themselves into the repair of homes which had been looted or burned. Moslem refugees from eastern Bosnia filled the void left by pre-war Serb residents.
Grbavica's skyscrapers, feared during the war for sheltering deadly Serb snipers, now have fresh laundry to display from their windows.

The Karamehmedovic family returned to their apartment last March to find empty walls stripped of window frames, doors and even sockets. It took five months and 4,000 marks ($2,380) to make their home habitable again.
"We are very lucky to be living back in our flat. Like other refugees, we thought we would never come back, but that has passed," Behija Karamehmedovic, 64, said.
Restoring a flat proved easier than rebuilding a scorched house, as the Pecar family discovered.
While Grbavica's apartment blocks quickly attracted donations and thousands of residents, many privately owned houses in Vrace hill above still await repair.
The three Pecar brothers found their houses burned to the ground. "I still cannot live in my house because the 15,000 marks I need to repair it have not appeared yet," said Sead Pecar.
Sead comes to visit the shell of his house every day and tends a little garden nearby.
"It will take many years to repair four years of damage," Sead mused. "But as long as we are alive there is hope."
